headline: RBI WPS (DEPR): 01/2026: Data Gaps in State-Level Inflation: An Assessment for the Covid Period
summary: Press Release RBI Working Paper Series No. 01 Data Gaps in State-Level Inflation: An Assessment for the Covid Period Purnima Shaw and R. K. Sinha @ Abstract 1 The disruption during Covid-19 necessitated statistical organisations across the world to impute the missing official statistics data or explore alternative data sources. The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) Inflation Expectations Survey of Households (IESH) continued to be conducted (using telephonic interviews) during the pandemic months. While imputed figures for the official price indices are available at the aggregate level for April and May 2020, the State-wise inflation data remains unpublished (missing) for four of the pandemic months. This paper uses granular IESH data and takes a distributional approach to provide State-wise inflation estimates for these data gaps. These State-wise inflation estimates when aggregated, closely follow the all-India official CPI inflation series. JEL Classification: D84, E17, E31 Keywords: Consumer price index, distribution function, inflation, inflation expectations Introduction The outbreak of the coronavirus (Covid-19) pandemic across the globe and the related administrative measures implemented to control its spread, e.g., closure of non-essential businesses, public offices and restricted movements resulted in a severe disturbance in the routine compilation and dissemination of official statistics. In such a scenario, the compilers of official statistics, like Central Banks and National Statistical Offices across the world needed to retain the confidence of the users of official statistics in the data. summary: It is my pleasure to be here at the SBI’s 13 th Banking and Economics conclave to share my views on the Indian economy and put them in the global context-- a context that is becoming increasingly more volatile and complex. In my brief comments, I will discuss the challenges that the global economic backdrop has posed for all emerging markets including India, how the Indian policymakers have addressed these challenges to both alleviate immediate pain and turn them into opportunities, and what the near future may look like for us. I. The Global Context 2. The global economic context has become less conducive since the global financial crisis of 2008-09. Several structural shifts have impacted the growth and policy outlook for emerging market economies, including peaking of global trade, ageing societies, climate risks, and stretched public finances. While the COVID crisis of 2020-21 added an unprecedented layer of shock and complexity to the global backdrop, a fresh wave of shocks since 2022, has further aggravated it. These recent shocks include two back-to-back commodity and energy shocks amidst unending geopolitical conflicts, policy uncertainty and tariff-led disruptions in trade; an El Niño event; tech-related developments and disruptions - led by AI. 3. India has perhaps been among the most challenged emerging market economies over past year and a half. Whereas most other countries were subject to only a subset of these shocks, India has been subjected to each one of these shocks –simultaneously and cumulatively. On trade, it had faced among the highest tariffs rates the US had imposed on any partner country and an acute policy uncertainty. headline: Supersession of Board of Directors of Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank Ltd., Mumbai - Extension of period
summary: The Reserve Bank of India, in exercise of its powers under Section 36AAA read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, had superseded the Board of Directors of Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank Ltd., Mumbai (the bank) for one year on November 24, 2023 , due to material concerns arising from poor governance standards observed within the bank . The period of supersession was extended for a period of one-year, effective November 24, 2024 and further extended for a period of one year, effective November 24, 2025 . 2. Upon a review, the Reserve Bank of India is satisfied that, in the public interest, it is necessary to further extend the period of supersession beyond the close of business of the bank as on November 23, 2026. 3. Accordingly, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), in exercise of its powers under sub-Section (1) of Section 36AAA read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, has extended the period of supersession for a further period of one-year, effective from November 24, 2026. Consequently, Shri Satya Prakash Pathak shall continue as the Administrator of the bank and shall be assisted by the present Committee of Advisors comprising of Shri Venkatesh Hegde, Shri Devendra Kumar, and Shri Suhas Gokhale. headline: Preserving Financial Stability in an Evolving World - Special Address by Shri Sanjay Malhotra, Governor, Reserve Bank of India, at the Fifth Kautilya Economic Conclave on October 3, 2026 -
summary: Thank you for inviting me to speak today. 2. I would like to speak on financial stability, the institutional mechanism, approach and tools for financial stability in our country, the emerging global risks, and our assessment of the financial system. I. What is Financial Stability? 3. As we all know, financial stability is the ability of the financial system to facilitate and enhance economic and financial transactions, manage risks, and absorb shocks 1 . A stable financial system is one in which financial intermediaries, markets and market infrastructures reliably provide the financial services that households and businesses depend on, including during periods of economic and financial market stress. It is a system in which households and businesses have the ability and confidence to save, borrow, invest, insure, make payments, manage risk and plan for the future 2 . II. Why financial stability? 4. One may ask the question: why talk about financial stability when the global financial system, despite repeated shocks, has been rather resilient and financial markets orderly. India too has had a stable financial system and among the strongest balance-sheets – of banks, corporates, governments and households – for a long period of time. 5. In fact, it is these very prolonged periods of stability that can encourage risk-taking and leverage, while fading memories of past crises can weaken the appetite for prudence, as Minsky's Financial Instability Hypothesis 3 reminds us. 6. I say this not because we see signs of any imminent stress but because we need to remind ourselves to remain alert to the risks. headline: Economic Resilience, Thinner Buffers, Emerging Risks Globally: Where Does India Stand?<sup>[1]</sup> - Address by Dr. Poonam Gupta, Deputy Governor, Reserve Bank of India, at the Business Standard BFSI Insight Summit -
summary: It is a pleasure to be back at the Business Standard BFSI Insight Summit. When I spoke here last year, my theme was the macroeconomic resilience of emerging markets (EMs), including India, which I attributed to the sound policy frameworks that these economies have adopted and adhered to. A year on, the resilience of the world economy has held. In today’s talk, I will reflect on the latest global outlook drawing on the recent publications of the IMF, how India is placed in this global context, and what policy priorities may be warranted for other EMs as well as India at this point in time. My observations are in four parts, one each on growth, inflation, public finances and the financial sector. 1. Growth rates seem resilient across countries The IMF’s latest World Economic Outlook (WEO, October 2026) projects the global economy to grow at 3.1 per cent in 2026 and 3.4 per cent in 2027. The projection for 2026 is 0.1 percentage point higher than in July, and that for 2027 is unchanged. While these numbers are below the pre-pandemic (2000–19) average of 3.7 per cent and the 2022–25 average of 3.5 per cent, they show continued resilience, given the underlying challenges the global economy has been facing. 2 In fact, actual growth has turned out stronger than projected by the IMF in each of the past three years, even as shocks have accumulated and intensified. A few more features of the latest projection deserve attention. First, the latest upgrade is accounted for by advanced economies (AEs), whose growth projection for 2026 has been raised by 0.4 percentage point to 2.1 per cent.
